entries.2128cd6320bada775429211e3cbd930e9bdced78: <div sID="gen18083" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="44" osisID="Jer.44" sID="Jer.44"/> <div eID="gen18083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18084" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18085" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. An awakening sermon which Jeremiah preaches to the Jews in Egypt, to reprove them for their idolatry, notwithstanding the warnings given them both by the word and the rod of God and to threaten the judgments of God against them for it, <reference osisRef="Jer.44.1-Jer.44.14">ver. 1-14</reference>. II. The impudent and impious contempt which the people put upon this admonition, and their declared resolution to persist in their idolatries notwithstanding, in despite of God and Jeremiah, <reference osisRef="Jer.44.15-Jer.44.19">ver. 15-19</reference>. III. The sentence passed upon them for their obstinacy, that they should all be cut off and perish in Egypt except a very small number; and, as a sign or earnest of it, the king of Egypt should shortly fall into the hands of the king of Babylon and be unable any longer to protect them, <reference osisRef="Jer.44.20-Jer.44.30">ver. 20-30</reference>.
entries.ab9895ef7b97469aaf8969675f5c9e593f9430f2: <div eID="gen18085" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18084" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Sermon to the Jews in Egypt; Jeremiah's Remonstrance. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 587.)</title> <div sID="gen18086" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the Jews which dwell in the land of Egypt, which dwell at Migdol, and at Tahpanhes, and at Noph, and in the country of Pathros, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, the God of Israel; Ye have seen all the evil that I have brought upon Jerusalem, and upon all the cities of Judah; and, behold, this day they <hi type="italic">are</hi> a desolation, and no man dwelleth therein, <hi type="super">3</hi> Because of their wickedness which they have committed to provoke me to anger, in that they went to burn incense, <hi type="italic">and</hi> to serve other gods, whom they knew not, <hi type="italic">neither</hi> they, ye, nor your fathers. <hi type="super">4</hi> Howbeit I sent unto you all my servants the prophets, rising early and sending <hi type="italic">them,</hi> saying, Oh, do not this abominable thing that I hate. <hi type="super">5</hi> But they hearkened not, nor inclined their ear to turn from their wickedness, to burn no incense unto other gods. <hi type="super">6</hi> Wherefore my fury and mine anger was poured forth, and was kindled in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem; and they are wasted <hi type="italic">and</hi> desolate, as at this day. <hi type="super">7</hi> Therefore now thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , the God of hosts, the God of Israel; Wherefore commit ye <hi type="italic">this</hi> great evil against your souls, to cut off from you man and woman, child and suckling, out of Judah, to leave you none to remain; <hi type="super">8</hi> In that ye provoke me unto wrath with the works of your hands, burning incense unto other gods in the land of Egypt, whither ye be gone to dwell, that ye might cut yourselves off, and that ye might be a curse and a reproach among all the nations of the earth? <hi type="super">9</hi> Have ye forgotten the wickedness of your fathers, and the wickedness of the kings of Judah, and the wickedness of their wives, and your own wickedness, and the wickedness of your wives, which they have committed in the land of Judah, and in the streets of Jerusalem? <hi type="super">10</hi> They are not humbled <hi type="italic">even</hi> unto this day, neither have they feared, nor walked in my law, nor in my statutes, that I set before you and before your fathers. <hi type="super">11</hi> Therefore thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, the God of Israel; Behold, I will set my face against you for evil, and to cut off all Judah. <hi type="super">12</hi> And I will take the remnant of Judah, that have set their faces to go into the land of Egypt to sojourn there, and they shall all be consumed, <hi type="italic">and</hi> fall in the land of Egypt; they shall <hi type="italic">even</hi> be consumed by the sword <hi type="italic">and</hi> by the famine: they shall die, from the least even unto the greatest, by the sword and by the famine: and they shall be an execration, <hi type="italic">and</hi> an astonishment, and a curse, and a reproach. <hi type="super">13</hi> For I will punish them that dwell in the land of Egypt, as I have punished Jerusalem, by the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence: <hi type="super">14</hi> So that none of the remnant of Judah, which are gone into the land of Egypt to sojourn there, shall escape or remain, that they should return into the land of Judah, to the which they have a desire to return to dwell there: for none shall return but such as shall escape. <div eID="gen18086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18087" type="x-p"/> The Jews in Egypt were now dispersed into various parts of the country, into <hi type="italic">Migdol, and Noph,</hi> and other places, and Jeremiah was sent on an errand from God to them, which he delivered either when he had the most of them together <hi type="italic">in Pathros</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.15">v. 15</reference>) or going about from place to place preaching to this purport. He delivered this message in the name of <hi type="italic">the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel,</hi> and in it, <div eID="gen18087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18088" type="x-p"/> I. God puts them in mind of the desolations of Judah and Jerusalem, which, though the captives <hi type="italic">by the rivers of Babylon</hi> were daily mindful of (<reference osisRef="Ps.137.1">Ps. cxxxvii. 1</reference>), the fugitives in the cities of Egypt seem to have forgotten and needed to be put in mind of, though, one would have thought, they had not been so long out of sight as to become out of mind (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">You have seen</hi> what a deplorable condition Judah and Jerusalem are brought into; now will you consider whence those desolations came? From the wrath of God; it was his fury and his anger that kindled the fire which made Jerusalem and <hi type="italic">the cities of Judah waste and desolate</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.6">v. 6</reference>); whoever were the instruments of the destruction, they were but instruments: it was a destruction from the Almighty. <div eID="gen18088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18089" type="x-p"/> II. He puts them in mind of the sins that brought those desolations upon Judah and Jerusalem. It was for <hi type="italic">their wickedness.</hi> It was this that <hi type="italic">provoked God to anger,</hi> and especially their idolatry, their <hi type="italic">serving other gods</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.3">v. 3</reference>) and giving that honour to counterfeit deities, the creatures of their own fancy and the work of their own hands, which should have been given to the true God only. They forsook the God who was known among them, and whose name was great, for gods that they knew not, upstart deities, whose original was obscure and not worth taking notice of: "<hi type="italic">Neither they nor you, nor your fathers,</hi> could give any rational account why <hi type="italic">the God of Israel</hi> was exchanged for such impostors." They knew not that they were gods; nay, they could not but know that they were no gods. <div eID="gen18089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18090" type="x-p"/> III. He puts them in mind of the frequent and fair warnings he had given them by his word not to serve other gods, the contempt of which warnings was a great aggravation of their idolatry, <reference osisRef="Jer.44.4">v. 4</reference>. <hi type="italic">The prophets</hi> were sent with a great deal of care to call to them, saying, <hi type="italic">Oh! do not this abominable thing that I hate.</hi> It becomes us to speak of sin with the utmost dread and detestation as an abominable thing; it is certainly so, for it is that which God hates, and we are sure that <hi type="italic">his judgment is according to truth.</hi> Call it grievous, call it odious, that we may by all means possible put ourselves and others out of love with it. It becomes us to give warning of the danger of sin, and the fatal consequences of it, with all seriousness and earnestness: "<hi type="italic">Oh! do not</hi> do it. If you love God, do not, for it is provoking to him; if you love your own souls do not, for it is destructive to them." Let conscience do this for us in an hour of temptation, when we are ready to yield. O take heed! <hi type="italic">do not this abominable thing</hi> which the Lord hates; for, if God hates it, thou shouldst hate it. But did they regard what God said to them? No: "<hi type="italic">They hearkened not, nor inclined their ear</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.5">v. 5</reference>); they still persisted in their idolatries; and you see what came of it, therefore God's <hi type="italic">anger was poured</hi> out upon them, <hi type="italic">as at this day.</hi> Now this was intended for warning to you, who have not only heard the judgments of God's mouth, as they did, but have likewise seen the judgments of his hand, by which you should be startled and awakened, for they were inflicted <hi type="italic">in terrorem,</hi> that others might hear and fear and do no more as they did, lest they should fare as they fared." <div eID="gen18090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18091" type="x-p"/> IV. He reproves them for, and upbraids them with, their continued idolatries, now that they had come into Egypt (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.8">v. 8</reference>): You <hi type="italic">burn incense to other gods in the land of Egypt. Therefore</hi> God forbade them to go into Egypt, because he knew it would be a snare to them. Those whom God sent into the land of the Chaldeans, though that was an idolatrous country, were there, by the power of God's grace, weaned from idolatry; but those who went against God's mind into the land of the Egyptians were there, by the power of their own corruptions, more wedded than ever to their idolatries; for, when we thrust ourselves without cause or call into places of temptation, it is just with God to leave us to ourselves. In doing this, 1. They did a great deal of injury to themselves and their families: "<hi type="italic">You commit this great evil against your souls</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.7">v. 7</reference>), you wrong them, you deceive them with that which is false, you destroy them, for it will be fatal to them." Note, In sinning against God we sin <hi type="italic">against our own souls.</hi> "It is the ready way to <hi type="italic">cut yourselves off</hi> from all comfort and hope (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.8">v. 8</reference>), to cut off your name and honour; so that you will, both by your sin and by your misery, become <hi type="italic">a curse and a reproach among all nations.</hi> It will become a proverb, As wretched as a Jew. It is the ready way <hi type="italic">to cut off from you</hi> all your relations, all that you should have joy of and have your families built up in, <hi type="italic">man and woman, child and suckling,</hi> so that Judah shall be a land lost for want of heirs." 2. They filled up the measure of the iniquity of their fathers, and, as if that had been too little for them, added to it (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.9">v. 9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Have you forgotten the wickedness</hi> of those who are gone before you, that you are not humbled for it as you ought to be, and afraid of the consequences of it?" <hi type="italic">Have you forgotten the punishments of your fathers?</hi> so some read it. "Do you not know how dear their idolatry cost them? And yet dare you continue in that vain conversation received by tradition from you fathers, though you received the curse with it?" He reminds them of the sins and punishments <hi type="italic">of the kings of Judah,</hi> who, great as they were, escaped not the judgments of God for their idolatry; yea, and they should have taken warning by <hi type="italic">the wickedness of their wives,</hi> who had seduced them to idolatry. In the original it is, <hi type="italic">And of his wives,</hi> which, Dr. Lightfoot thinks, tacitly reflects upon Solomon's wives, particularly his Egyptian wives, to whom the idolatry of the kings of Judah owed its original. "Have you forgotten this, and what came of it, that you dare venture upon the same wicked courses?" See <reference osisRef="Neh.13.18">Neh. xiii. 18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.26">26</reference>. "Nay, to come to your own times, <hi type="italic">Have you forgotten your own wickedness and the wickedness of your wives,</hi> when you lived in prosperity in Jerusalem, and what ruin it brought upon you? But, alas! to what purpose do I speak to them?" (says God to the prophet, <reference osisRef="Jer.44.10">v. 10</reference>) "<hi type="italic">they are not humbled unto this day,</hi> by all the humbling providences that they have been under. <hi type="italic">They have not feared, nor walked in my law.</hi>" Note, Those that walk not in the law of God do thereby show that they are destitute of the fear of God. <div eID="gen18091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18092" type="x-p"/> V. He threatens their utter ruin for their persisting in their idolatry now that they were in Egypt. Judgment is given against them, as before (<reference osisRef="Jer.42.22">ch. xlii. 22</reference>), that they shall perish in Egypt; the decree has gone forth, and shall not be called back. They <hi type="italic">set their faces to go into the land of Egypt</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.12">v. 12</reference>), were resolute in their purpose against God, and now God is resolute in his purpose against them: <hi type="italic">I will set my face to cut off all Judah,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.44.11">v. 11</reference>. Those that think not only to affront, but to confront, God Almighty, will find themselves outfaced; for <hi type="italic">the face of the Lord is against those that do evil,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.34.16">Ps. xxxiv. 16</reference>. It is here threatened concerning these idolatrous Jews in Egypt, 1. That <hi type="italic">they shall all be consumed,</hi> without exception; no degree nor order among them shall escape: <hi type="italic">They shall fall, from the least to the greatest</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.12">v. 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">high and low, rich and poor.</hi> 2. That <hi type="italic">they shall be consumed by</hi> the very same judgments which God made use of for the punishment of Jerusalem, <hi type="italic">the sword, famine, and pestilence,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.44.12-Jer.44.13">v. 12, 13</reference>. They shall not be wasted by natural deaths, as Israel in the wilderness, but by these sore judgments, which, by flying into Egypt, they thought to get out of the reach of. 3. That none (except a very few that will narrowly escape) shall ever <hi type="italic">return to the land of Judah</hi> again, <reference osisRef="Jer.44.14">v. 14</reference>. They thought, being nearer, that they stood fairer for a return to their own land than those that were carried to Babylon; yet those shall return, and these shall not; for the way in which God has promised us any comfort is much surer than that in which we have projected it for ourselves. Observe, Those that are fretful and discontented will be uneasy and fond of change wherever they are. The Israelites, when they were in the land of Judah, desired to go into Egypt (<reference osisRef="Jer.42.22">ch. xlii. 22</reference>), but when they were in Egypt they desired to <hi type="italic">return to the land of Judah</hi> again; they <hi type="italic">lifted up their soul</hi> to it (so it is in the margin), which denotes an earnest desire. But, because they would not dwell there when God commanded it, they shall not dwell they were they desire it. If we walk contrary to God, he will walk contrary to us. How can those expect to be well off who would not know when they were so, though God himself told them?
entries.c265500c161940c234045aa0dec6b40d5356694a: <div eID="gen18092" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The People's Insolent Reply. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 587.)</title> <div sID="gen18093" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> Then all the men which knew that their wives had burned incense unto other gods, and all the women that stood by, a great multitude, even all the people that dwelt in the land of Egypt, in Pathros, answered Jeremiah, saying, <hi type="super">16</hi> <hi type="italic">As for</hi> the word that thou hast spoken unto us in the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , we will not hearken unto thee. <hi type="super">17</hi> But we will certainly do whatsoever thing goeth forth out of our own mouth, to burn incense unto the queen of heaven, and to pour out drink offerings unto her, as we have done, we, and our fathers, our kings, and our princes, in the cities of Judah, and in the streets of Jerusalem: for <hi type="italic">then</hi> had we plenty of victuals, and were well, and saw no evil. <hi type="super">18</hi> But since we left off to burn incense to the queen of heaven, and to pour out drink offerings unto her, we have wanted all <hi type="italic">things,</hi> and have been consumed by the sword and by the famine. <hi type="super">19</hi> And when we burned incense to the queen of heaven, and poured out drink offerings unto her, did we make her cakes to worship her, and pour out drink offerings unto her, without our men? <div eID="gen18093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18094" type="x-p"/> We have here the people's obstinate refusal to submit to the power of the word of God in the mouth of Jeremiah. We have scarcely such an instance of downright daring contradiction to God himself as this, or such an avowed rebellion of the carnal mind. Observe, <div eID="gen18094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18095" type="x-p"/> I. The persons who thus set God and his judgments at defiance; it was not some one that was thus obstinate, but the generality of the Jews; and they were such as knew either themselves or their wives to be guilty of the idolatry Jeremiah had reproved, <reference osisRef="Jer.44.15">v. 15</reference>. We find, 1. That the women had been more guilty of idolatry and superstition than the men, not because the men stuck closer to the true God and the true religion than the women, but, I fear, because they were generally atheists, and were for no God and no religion at all, and therefore could easily allow their wives to be of a false religion, and to worship false gods. 2. That it was consciousness of guilt that made them impatient of reproof: <hi type="italic">They knew that their wives had burnt incense to other gods,</hi> and that they had countenanced them in it, <hi type="italic">and the women that stood by</hi> knew that they had joined with them in their idolatrous usages; so that what Jeremiah said touched them in a sore place, which made them <hi type="italic">kick against the pricks,</hi> as <hi type="italic">children of Belial,</hi> that will not <hi type="italic">bear the yoke.</hi> <div eID="gen18095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18096" type="x-p"/> II. The reply which these persons made to Jeremiah, and in him to God himself; it is in effect the same with theirs who had the impudence to say to the Almighty, <hi type="italic">Depart from us; we desire not the knowledge of thy ways.</hi> <div eID="gen18096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18097" type="x-p"/> 1. They declare their resolution not to do as God commanded them, but what they themselves had a mind to do; that is, they would go on to worship the moon, here called <hi type="italic">the queen of heaven;</hi> yet some understand it of the sun, which was much worshipped in Egypt (<reference osisRef="Jer.43.13">ch. xliii. 13</reference>) and had been so at Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.11">2 Kings xxiii. 11</reference>), and they say that the Hebrew word for the sun being feminine it may not unfitly be called <hi type="italic">the queen of heaven.</hi> And others understand it of all <hi type="italic">the host of heaven,</hi> or <hi type="italic">the frame of heaven,</hi> the whole machine, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.18">ch. vii. 18</reference>. These daring sinners do not now go about to make excuses for their refusal to obey, nor suggest that Jeremiah spoke from himself and not from God (as before, <reference osisRef="Jer.43.2">ch. xliii. 2</reference>), but they own that he spoke to them <hi type="italic">in the name of the Lord,</hi> and yet tell him flatly, in so many words, "<hi type="italic">We will not hearken unto thee;</hi> we will do that which is forbidden and run the hazard of that which is threatened." Note, Those that live in disobedience to God commonly grow worse and worse, and the heart is more and more hardened by <hi type="italic">the deceitfulness of sin.</hi> Here is the genuine language of the rebellious heart: <hi type="italic">We will certainly do whatsoever thing goes forth out of our own mouth,</hi> let God and his prophets say what they please to the contrary. What they said many think who yet have not arrived at such a degree of impudence as to speak it out. It is that which the young man would be at <hi type="italic">in the days of his youth;</hi> he would <hi type="italic">walk in the way of his heart and the sight of his eyes,</hi> and would have and do every thing he has a mind to, <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.9">Eccl. xi. 9</reference>. <div eID="gen18097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18098" type="x-p"/> 2. They give some sort of reasons for their resolution; for the most absurd and unreasonably wicked men will have something to say for themselves, till the day comes when <hi type="italic">every mouth shall be stopped.</hi> <div eID="gen18098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18099" type="x-p"/> (1.) They plead many of those things which the advocates for Rome make the marks of a true church, and not only justify but magnify themselves with; and these Jews have as much right to them as the Romanists have. [1.] They plead antiquity: We are resolved <hi type="italic">to burn incense to the queen of heaven,</hi> for <hi type="italic">our fathers</hi> did so; it is a practice that pleads prescription; and why should we pretend to be wiser than our fathers? [2.] They plead authority. Those that had power practised it themselves and prescribed it to others: <hi type="italic">Our kings and our princes</hi> did it, whom God set over us, and who were of the seed of David. [3.] They plead unity. It was not here and there one that did it, but <hi type="italic">we,</hi> we all with one consent, we that are <hi type="italic">a great multitude</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.15">v. 15</reference>), we did it. [4.] They plead universality. It was not done here and there, but <hi type="italic">in the cities of Judah.</hi> [5.] They plead visibility. It was not done in a corner, in dark and shady groves only, but <hi type="italic">in the streets,</hi> openly and publicly. [6.] They plead that it was the practice of the mother-church, the holy see; it was not now learned first in Egypt, but it had been done in <hi type="italic">Jerusalem.</hi> [7.] They plead prosperity: <hi type="italic">They had we plenty of</hi> bread, <hi type="italic">and</hi> of all good things; we <hi type="italic">were well and saw no evil.</hi> All the former pleas, I fear, were too true in fact; God's witnesses against their idolatry were few and hid; Elijah though that he was left alone: and this last might perhaps be true as to some particular persons, but, as to their nation, they were still under rebukes for their rebellions, and there was <hi type="italic">no peace to those that went out or came in,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.5">2 Chron. xv. 5</reference>. But, supposing all to be true, yet this does not at all excuse them from idolatry; it is the law of God that we must be ruled and judged by, not the practice of men. <div eID="gen18099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18100" type="x-p"/> (2.) They suggest that the judgments they had of late been under were brought upon them for <hi type="italic">leaving off to burn incense to the queen of heaven,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.44.18">v. 18</reference>. So perversely did they misconstrue providence, though God, by his prophets, had so often explained it to them, and the thing itself spoke the direct contrary. <hi type="italic">Since we</hi> forsook our idolatries <hi type="italic">we have wanted all things, and have been consumed by the sword,</hi> the true reason of which was because they still retained their idols in their heart and an affection to their old sins; but they would have it thought that it was because they had forsaken the acts of sin. Thus the afflictions which should have been for their welfare, to separate between them and their sins, being misinterpreted did but confirm them in their sins. Thus, in the first ages of Christianity, when God chastised the nations by any public calamities for opposing the Christians and persecuting them, they put a contrary sense upon the calamities, as if they were sent to punish them for conniving at the Christians and tolerating them, and cried, <hi type="italic">Christianos ad leones—Throw the Christians to the lions.</hi> Yet, if it had been true, as they said here, that since they returned to the service of the true God, the God of Israel, they had been in want and trouble, was that a reason why they should revolt from him again? That was as much as to say that they served not him, but their own bellies. Those who know God, and put their trust in him, will serve him, though he starve them, though he slay them, though they never see a good day with him in this world, being well assured that they shall not lose by him in the end. <div eID="gen18100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18101" type="x-p"/> (3.) They plead that, though the women were most forward and active in their idolatries, yet they did it with the consent and approbation of their husbands; the women were busy to <hi type="italic">make cakes</hi> for meat-offerings <hi type="italic">to the queen of heaven</hi> and to prepare <hi type="italic">and pour out the drink-offerings,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.44.19">v. 19</reference>. We found, before, that this was their work, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.18">ch. vii. 18</reference>. "But <hi type="italic">did we</hi> do it <hi type="italic">without our husbands,</hi> privately and unknown to them, so as to give them occasion to be jealous of us? No; the fathers kindled the fire while the women kneaded the dough; the men that were our heads, whom we were bound to learn of and to be obedient to, taught us to do it by their example." Note, It is sad when those who are in the nearest relation to each other, who should quicken each other to that which is good and so help one another to heaven, harden each other in sin and so ripen one another for hell. Some understand this as spoken by the husbands (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.15">v. 15</reference>), who plead that they did not do it <hi type="italic">without their men,</hi> that is, without their elders and rulers, their great men, and men in authority; but, because the making of the <hi type="italic">cakes</hi> and the pouring out of the <hi type="italic">drink-offerings</hi> are expressly spoken of as the women's work (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.18">ch. vii. 18</reference>), it seems rather to be understood as their plea: but it was a frivolous plea. What would it avail them to be able to say that it was according to their husbands' mind, when they knew that it was contrary to their God's mind?
entries.590e7c7df8a6ed68eab350e4efd7797ed1b6d5df: <div eID="gen18101" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Jeremiah's Continued Remonstrance. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 587.)</title> <div sID="gen18102" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> Then Jeremiah said unto all the people, to the men, and to the women, and to all the people which had given him <hi type="italic">that</hi> answer, saying, <hi type="super">21</hi> The incense that ye burned in the cities of Judah, and in the streets of Jerusalem, ye, and your fathers, your kings, and your princes, and the people of the land, did not the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> remember them, and came it <hi type="italic">not</hi> into his mind? <hi type="super">22</hi> So that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> could no longer bear, because of the evil of your doings, <hi type="italic">and</hi> because of the abominations which ye have committed; therefore is your land a desolation, and an astonishment, and a curse, without an inhabitant, as at this day. <hi type="super">23</hi> Because ye have burned incense, and because ye have sinned against the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and have not obeyed the voice of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , nor walked in his law, nor in his statutes, nor in his testimonies; therefore this evil is happened unto you, as at this day. <hi type="super">24</hi> Moreover Jeremiah said unto all the people, and to all the women, Hear the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , all Judah that <hi type="italic">are</hi> in the land of Egypt: <hi type="super">25</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, the God of Israel, saying; Ye and your wives have both spoken with your mouths, and fulfilled with your hand, saying, We will surely perform our vows that we have vowed, to burn incense to the queen of heaven, and to pour out drink offerings unto her: ye will surely accomplish your vows, and surely perform your vows. <hi type="super">26</hi> Therefore hear ye the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , all Judah that dwell in the land of Egypt; Behold, I have sworn by my great name, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , that my name shall no more be named in the mouth of any man of Judah in all the land of Egypt, saying, The Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> liveth. <hi type="super">27</hi> Behold, I will watch over them for evil, and not for good: and all the men of Judah that <hi type="italic">are</hi> in the land of Egypt shall be consumed by the sword and by the famine, until there be an end of them. <hi type="super">28</hi> Yet a small number that escape the sword shall return out of the land of Egypt into the land of Judah, and all the remnant of Judah, that are gone into the land of Egypt to sojourn there, shall know whose words shall stand, mine, or theirs. <hi type="super">29</hi> And this <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> a sign unto you, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , that I will punish you in this place, that ye may know that my words shall surely stand against you for evil: <hi type="super">30</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; Behold, I will give Pharaoh-hophra king of Egypt into the hand of his enemies, and into the hand of them that seek his life; as I gave Zedekiah king of Judah into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, his enemy, and that sought his life. <div eID="gen18102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18103" type="x-p"/> Daring sinners may speak many a bold word and many a big word, but, after all, God will have the last word; for he will be justified when he speaks, and all flesh, even the proudest, shall be silent before him. Prophets may be run down, but God cannot; nay, here the prophet would not. <div eID="gen18103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18104" type="x-p"/> I. Jeremiah has something to say to them from himself, which he could say without a spirit of prophecy, and that was to rectify their mistake (a wilful mistake it was) concerning the calamities they had been under and the true intent and meaning of them. They said that these miseries came upon them because they had now <hi type="italic">left off burning incense to the queen of heaven.</hi> "No," says he, "it was because you had formerly done it, not because you had now left it off." When they gave him that answer, he immediately replied (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.20">v. 20</reference>) that the incense which they and their fathers had burnt to other gods did indeed go unpunished a great while, for God was long-suffering towards them, and during the day of his patience it was perhaps, as they said, <hi type="italic">well with them, and</hi> they <hi type="italic">saw no evil;</hi> but at length they grew so provoking <hi type="italic">that the Lord could no longer bear</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.22">v. 22</reference>), but began a controversy with them, whereupon some of them did a little reform; their sins left them, for so it might be said, rather than that they left their sins. But their old guilt being still upon the score, and their corrupt inclinations still the same, God remembered against them the idolatries of <hi type="italic">their fathers, their kings, and their princes, in the streets of Jerusalem,</hi> which they, instead of being ashamed of, gloried in as a justification of them in their idolatries; they <hi type="italic">all came into his mind</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.21">v. 21</reference>), all the <hi type="italic">abominations which they had committed</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.22">v. 22</reference>) and all their disobedience to <hi type="italic">the voice of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.23">v. 23</reference>), all were brought to account; and <hi type="italic">therefore,</hi> to punish them for these, <hi type="italic">is their land a desolation and a curse, as at this day</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.22">v. 22</reference>); <hi type="italic">therefore,</hi> not for their late reformation, but for their old transgressions, has all <hi type="italic">this evil happened to them, as at this day,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.44.23">v. 23</reference>. Note, The right understanding of the cause of our troubles, one would think, should go far towards the cure of our sins. Whatever <hi type="italic">evil comes upon us,</hi> it is <hi type="italic">because we have sinned against the Lord,</hi> and should therefore <hi type="italic">stand in awe and sin not.</hi> <div eID="gen18104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18105" type="x-p"/> II. Jeremiah has something to say to them, <hi type="italic">to the women</hi> particularly, from <hi type="italic">the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel,</hi> They have given their answer; now let them hear God's reply, <reference osisRef="Jer.44.24">v. 24</reference>. <hi type="italic">Judah, that</hi> dwells <hi type="italic">in the land of Egypt,</hi> has God speaking to them, even there; that is their privilege. Let them observe what he says; that is their duty, <reference osisRef="Jer.44.26">v. 26</reference>. Now God, in his reply, tells them plainly, <div eID="gen18105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18106" type="x-p"/> 1. That, since they were fully determined to persist in their idolatry, he was fully determined to proceed in his controversy with them; if they would go on to provoke him, he would go on to punish them, and see which would get the better at last. God repeats what they had said (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.25">v. 25</reference>): "<hi type="italic">You and your wives</hi> are agreed in this obstinacy; <hi type="italic">you have spoken with your mouths and fulfilled with your hands;</hi> you have said it, and you stand to it, have said it and go on to do accordingly, <hi type="italic">We will surely perform our vows that we have vowed, to burn incense to the queen of heaven,</hi>" as if, though it were a sin, yet their having vowed to do it were sufficient to justify them in the doing of it; whereas no man can by his vow make that lawful to himself, much less duty, which God has already made sin. "Well" (says God), "<hi type="italic">you will accomplish, you will perform, your</hi> wicked <hi type="italic">vows:</hi> now hear what is my vow, what <hi type="italic">I have sworn by my great name;</hi>" and, if <hi type="italic">the Lord hath sworn,</hi> he <hi type="italic">will not repent,</hi> since they have sworn and will not repent. <hi type="italic">With the froward he will show himself froward,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.18.26">Ps. xviii. 26</reference>. (1.) He had sworn that what little remains of religion there were among them should be lost, <reference osisRef="Jer.44.26">v. 26</reference>. Though they joined with the Egyptians in their idolatries, yet they continued upon many occasions to make mention of the name of Jehovah, particularly in their solemn oaths; they said, <hi type="italic">Jehovah liveth,</hi> he is <hi type="italic">the living God,</hi> so they owned him to be, though they worshipped dead idols; they swear, <hi type="italic">The Lord liveth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.5.2">ch. v. 2</reference>), but I fear they retained this form of swearing more in honour of their nation than of their God. But God declares that his <hi type="italic">name shall no more be</hi> thus <hi type="italic">named</hi> by <hi type="italic">any man of Judah in all the land of Egypt;</hi> that is, there shall be no Jews remaining to use this dialect of their country, or, if there be, they shall have forgotten it and shall learn to swear, as the Egyptians do, <hi type="italic">by the life of Pharaoh,</hi> not of Jehovah. Note, Those are very miserable whom God has so far left to themselves that they have quite forgotten their religion and lost all the remains of their good education. Or this may intimate that God would take it as an affront to him and would resent it accordingly, if they did make mention of his name and profess any relation to him. (2.) He hath sworn that what little remnant of people there was there should all be consumed (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.27">v. 27</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will watch over them for evil;</hi> no opportunity shall be let slip to bring some judgment upon them, <hi type="italic">until there be an end of them</hi> and they be rooted out. Note, To those whom God finds impenitent sinners he will be found an implacable Judge. And, when it comes to this, they <hi type="italic">shall know</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.28">v. 28</reference>) <hi type="italic">whose word shall stand, mind or theirs.</hi> They said that they should recover themselves when they returned to worship <hi type="italic">the queen of heaven;</hi> God said they should ruin themselves; and now the event will show which was in the right. The contest between God and sinners is whose word shall stand, whose will shall be done, and who shall get the better. Sinners say that they shall have peace though they go on; God says they shall have no peace. But <hi type="italic">when God judges he will overcome;</hi> God's word shall stand, and not the sinner's. <div eID="gen18106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18107" type="x-p"/> 2. He tells them that a very few of them should <hi type="italic">escape the sword,</hi> and in process of time <hi type="italic">return into the land of Judah, a small number</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.28">v. 28</reference>), next to none, in comparison with the great numbers that should return out of the land of the Chaldeans. This seems designed to upbraid those who boasted of their numbers that concurred in sin; there were none to speak of that did not join in idolatry: "Well," says God, "and there shall be as few <hi type="italic">that</hi> shall <hi type="italic">escape the sword and famine.</hi>" <div eID="gen18107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18108" type="x-p"/> 3. He gives them a sign that all these threatenings shall be accomplished in their season, that they shall be consumed here in Egypt and shall quite perish: <hi type="italic">Pharaoh-hophra,</hi> the present <hi type="italic">king of Egypt,</hi> shall be delivered <hi type="italic">into the hand of his enemies that seek his life—of his own rebellious subjects</hi> (so some) under Amasis, who usurped his throne—<hi type="italic">of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon</hi> (so others), who invaded his kingdom; the former is related by Herodotus, the latter by Josephus. It is likely that this Pharaoh had tempted the Jews to idolatry by promises of his favour; however, they depended upon him for his protection, and it would be more than a presage of their ruin, it would be a step towards it, if he were gone. They expected more from him than from Zedekiah king of Judah; he was a more potent and politic prince. "But," says God, "<hi type="italic">I will give him into the hand of his enemies,</hi> as I gave Zedekiah." Note, Those creature-comforts and confidences that we promise ourselves most from may fail us as soon as those that we promise ourselves least from, for they are all what God makes them, not what we fancy them. <div eID="gen18108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18109" type="x-p"/> The sacred history records not the accomplishment of this prophecy, but its silence is sufficient; we hear no more of these Jews in Egypt, and therefore conclude them, according to this prediction, lost there; for no word of God shall fall to the ground.  <chapter eID="Jer.44"/> <div eID="gen18109" type="x-p"/>

entries.4512876113b71cac504a24e644092e316862d899: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10531"/><div sID="gen18775" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10531"/>9. Have you forgotten how the wickednesses of your fathers were the source of the greatest calamities to you?<div eID="gen18775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18776" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their wives--</hi>The Jews' worldly queens were great promoters of idolatry (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.1-1Kgs.8.15">1Ki 11:1-8; 15</reference>:13; 16:31).<div eID="gen18776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18777" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the land of Judah--</hi>They defiled the land which was holy unto God. <div eID="gen18777" type="x-p"/>
entries.1b33dacab799445515bd0a789348f327f35385c0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10532"/><div sID="gen18778" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10532"/><hi type="bold">10. They ... you--</hi>The third person puts them to a distance from God on account of their alienating themselves from Him. The second person implies that God formerly had directly addressed them.<div eID="gen18778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18779" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">humbled--</hi>literally, "contrite" (<reference osisRef="Ps.51.17">Psa 51:17</reference>).<div eID="gen18779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18780" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither ... feared--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Prov.28.14">Pr 28:14</reference>). <div eID="gen18780" type="x-p"/>
entries.75ae925034360e80417b7ebffd3133c8bc59ca87: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10533"/><div sID="gen18781" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10533"/><hi type="bold">11. Behold, I will set my face against you for evil--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Lev.17.10">Le 17:10</reference>).<div eID="gen18781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18782" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and to cut off all Judah--</hi>that is, all the idolaters; <reference osisRef="Jer.44.28">Jr 44:28</reference> shows that some returned to Judea (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.42.17">Jr 42:17</reference>). <div eID="gen18782" type="x-p"/>
entries.3ab443a08eff9aae6d5cb1bc694bf758ad2735d1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10534"/><div sID="gen18783" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10534"/><hi type="bold">14. none ... shall escape ... that they should return, &c.--</hi>The Jews had gone to Egypt with the idea that a return to Judea, which they thought hopeless to their brethren in Babylon, would be an easy matter to themselves in Egypt: the exact reverse should happen in the case of each respectively. The Jews whom God sent to Babylon were there weaned from idolatry, and were restored; those who went to Egypt by their perverse will were hardened in idolatry, and perished there.<div eID="gen18783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18784" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">have a desire--</hi>literally, "lift up (their) soul," that is, their hopes (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.22.27">Jr 22:27</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Deut.24.15">De 24:15</reference>, Margin).<div eID="gen18784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18785" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">none shall return but such as shall escape--</hi>namely, the "small number" (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.28">Jr 44:28</reference>) who were brought by force into Egypt, as Jeremiah and Baruch, and those who, in accordance with Jeremiah's advice, should flee from Egypt before the arrival of the Chaldeans (see on <reference osisRef="Jer.42.17">Jr 42:17</reference>). Calvin less probably refers the words to the return of the exiles in Babylon, which the Jews in Egypt regarded as hopeless. <div eID="gen18785" type="x-p"/>
entries.fe2adfb6fa159912fc9e9bfb6ef5ee5477f1906d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10535"/><div sID="gen18786" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10535"/><hi type="bold">15. their wives--</hi>The idolatry began with them (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.4">1Ki 11:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.14">1Ti 2:14</reference>). Their husbands' connivance implicated them in the guilt. <div eID="gen18786" type="x-p"/>
entries.44a741e8efccc791ed827e4872237878f63801de: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10536"/><div sID="gen18787" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10536"/><hi type="bold">16. we will not--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.6.16">Jr 6:16</reference>). <div eID="gen18787" type="x-p"/>
entries.67a1a8bbf5223601749475b7fd07b0de4bdacb6a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10537"/><div sID="gen18788" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10537"/><hi type="bold">17. whatsoever ... goeth ... out of our ... mouth--</hi>whatever vow we have uttered to our gods (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.25">Jr 44:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.23.23">De 23:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.11.36">Jud 11:36</reference>). The source of all superstitions is that men oppose their own will and fancies to God's commands.<div eID="gen18788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18789" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">queen of heaven--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Jer.7.18">Jr 7:18</reference>); Ashtaroth or Astarte.<div eID="gen18789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18790" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we ... fathers ... king, &c.--</hi>The evil was restricted to no one class: all from the highest to the lowest shared the guilt.<div eID="gen18790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18791" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">then had we plenty--</hi>Fools attribute their seeming prosperity to God's connivance at their sin: but see <reference osisRef="Prov.1.32">Pr 1:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.11-Eccl.8.13">Ec 8:11-13</reference>. In fact, God had often chastised them for their idolatry (see <reference osisRef="Judg.2.14">Jud 2:14</reference>); but it is the curse of impiety not to perceive the hand of God in calamities.<div eID="gen18791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18792" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">victuals--</hi>Men cast away the bread of the soul for the bread that perisheth (<reference osisRef="Deut.8.3">De 8:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.6.27">Joh 6:27</reference>). So Esau (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.16">He 12:16</reference>). <div eID="gen18792" type="x-p"/>
entries.02d45dcd080b5c4812808ff88f1ed2609adc6371: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10538"/><div sID="gen18793" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10538"/>18. They impute their calamities to their service of God, but these are often marks of His favor, not of wrath, to do His people good at their latter end (<reference osisRef="Deut.8.16">De 8:16</reference>). <div eID="gen18793" type="x-p"/>
entries.6282c381bc4bbe2c4ef65e003a00f9cdb5921e83: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10539"/><div sID="gen18794" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10539"/><hi type="bold">19. make ... cakes to worship her--</hi>Maurer translates, "to form her image." Crescent-shaped cakes were offered to the moon. Vulgate supports English Version.<div eID="gen18794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18795" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">without our men--</hi>The women mentioned (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.15">Jr 44:15</reference>); "a great multitude" here speak: we have not engaged in secret night orgies which might justly be regarded unfavorably by our husbands: our sacred rites have been open, and with their privity. They wish to show how unreasonable it is that Jeremiah should oppose himself alone to the act of all, not merely women, but men also. The guilty, like these women, desire to shield themselves under the complicity of others. Instead of helping one another towards heaven, husband and wife often ripen one another for hell. <div eID="gen18795" type="x-p"/>
entries.064b93638a34dcd8ea4c30b5cc3a3cd67905845a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10540"/><div sID="gen18796" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10540"/><hi type="bold">21. The incense ... did not the Lord remember--</hi>Jeremiah owns that they did as they said, but in retort asks, did not God repay their own evil-doing? Their very land in its present desolation attests this (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.22">Jr 44:22</reference>), as was foretold (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.11">Jr 25:11</reference>, 18, 38). <div eID="gen18796" type="x-p"/>
entries.fb2d2f8aa2b4d0f9b1aa4e7c474a0647897ad785: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10541"/><div sID="gen18797" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10541"/><hi type="bold">23. law--</hi>the moral precepts.<div eID="gen18797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18798" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">statutes--</hi>the ceremonial.<div eID="gen18798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18799" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">testimonies--</hi>the judicial (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.11">Da 9:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.9.12">12</reference>). <div eID="gen18799" type="x-p"/>
entries.24036f6875d465ea0f2e528dada95c51f1a5bc68: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10542"/><div sID="gen18800" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10542"/><hi type="bold">25. Ye ... have both spoken with ... mouths, and fulfilled with ... hand--</hi>ironical praise. They had pleaded their obligation to fulfil their vows, in excuse for their idolatry. He answers, no one can accuse you of unsteadiness as to your idolatrous vows; but steadfastness towards God ought to have prevented you from making, or, when made, from keeping such vows.<div eID="gen18800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18801" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye will surely accomplish ... vows--</hi>Jeremiah hereby gives them up to their own fatal obstinacy. <div eID="gen18801" type="x-p"/>
entries.8f5d332ec53fe8e327bc2156330f9992026259b6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10543"/><div sID="gen18802" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10543"/><hi type="bold">26. I have sworn--</hi>I, too have made a vow which I will fulfil. Since ye will not hear Me speaking and warning, hear Me swearing.<div eID="gen18802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18803" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by my great name--</hi>that is, by Myself (<reference osisRef="Gen.22.16">Ge 22:16</reference>), the greatest by whom God can swear (<reference osisRef="Heb.6.13">He 6:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.6.14">14</reference>).<div eID="gen18803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18804" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my name shall no more be named--</hi>The Jews, heretofore, amidst all their idolatry, had retained the form of appeal to the name of God and the law, the distinctive glory of their nation; God will allow this no more (<reference osisRef="Ezek.20.39">Eze 20:39</reference>): there shall be none left there to profane His name thus any more. <div eID="gen18804" type="x-p"/>
entries.31627a604482f7be273c24ad04b3276d6a4b4b85: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10544"/><div sID="gen18805" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10544"/><hi type="bold">27. watch over ... for evil--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.1.10">Jr 1:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.6">Eze 7:6</reference>). The God, whose providence is ever solicitously watching over His people for good, shall solicitously, as it were, watch for their hurt. Contrast <reference osisRef="Jer.31.28">Jr 31:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.32.41">32:41</reference>. <div eID="gen18805" type="x-p"/>
entries.80ab46572c34c14748c46fb8752558e1db9f27fa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10545"/><div sID="gen18806" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10545"/><hi type="bold">28. small number--</hi>(see on <reference osisRef="Jer.44.14">Jr 44:14</reference>; and <reference osisRef="Jer.42.17">Jr 42:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.27.13">Is 27:13</reference>); compare "all-consumed" (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.27">Jr 44:27</reference>). A band easily counted, whereas they were expecting to return triumphantly in large numbers.<div eID="gen18806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18807" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall know--</hi>most of them experimentally, and to their cost.<div eID="gen18807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18808" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whose words ... mine, or theirs--</hi>Hebrew, "that from Me and them." Jehovah's words are His threats of destruction to the Jews; theirs, the assertion that they expected all goods from their gods (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.17">Jr 44:17</reference>), &c. "Mine"; by which I predict ruin to them. "Theirs"; by which they give themselves free scope in iniquity.<div eID="gen18808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18809" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall stand--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.33.11">Psa 33:11</reference>). <div eID="gen18809" type="x-p"/>
entries.6012bec2fa611bd92ddfd2ac295418444dd9355b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10546"/><div sID="gen18810" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10546"/><hi type="bold">29. this ... sign unto you--</hi>The calamity of Pharaoh-hophra (see on <reference osisRef="Jer.44.30">Jr 44:30</reference>) shall be a sign to you that as he shall fall before his enemy, so you shall subsequently fall before Nebuchadnezzar (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.8">Mt 24:8</reference>) [Grotius]. Calvin makes the "sign" to be simultaneous with the event signified, not antecedent to it, as in <reference osisRef="Exod.3.12">Ex 3:12</reference>. The Jews believed Egypt impregnable, so shut in was it by natural barriers. The Jews being "punished in this place" will be a sign that their view is false, and God's threat true. He calls it "a sign unto you," because God's prediction is equivalent to the event, so that they may even now take it as a sign. When fulfilled it would cease to be a sign to them: for they would be dead. <div eID="gen18810" type="x-p"/>
entries.dc1ba75cddf1533ac22b85ba210ce7d18950075c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10547"/><div sID="gen18811" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10547"/><hi type="bold">30. Hophra--</hi>in Herodotus called Apries. He succeeded Psammis, the successor of Pharaoh-necho, who was beaten by Nebuchadnezzar at Carchemish, on the Euphrates. Amasis rebelled against, and overcame him, in the city Sais.<div eID="gen18811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18812" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">them that seek his life--</hi>Herodotus, in curious accordance with this, records that Amasis, after treating Hophra well at first, was instigated, by persons who thought they could not be safe unless he were put to death, to strangle him. "His enemies" refer to Amasis, &c.; the words are accurately chosen, so as not to refer to Nebuchadnezzar, who is not mentioned till the end of the verse, and in connection with Zedekiah (<reference osisRef="Ezek.20.3">Eze 20:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.21">30:21</reference>). Amasis' civil war with Hophra pioneered the way for Nebuchadnezzar's invasion in the twenty-third year of his reign [Josephus, Antiquities, 10.11]. <chapter eID="Jer.44"/>

entries.e52598297a63aaba2971f0e2daf66ae5bafbabf6: <div eID="gen30472" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen30473" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen30474" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30474" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30473" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen30475" type="x-p"/> Jeremiah reproves the Jews in Egypt for continuing in idolatry after the exemplary judgments indicted by God on their nation for that sin, <reference osisRef="Jer.44.1-Jer.44.14">Jer 44:1-14</reference>; and, upon their refusing to reform, denounces destruction to them, and to that kingdom wherein they sought protection, vv. 15-30. <div eID="gen30475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30476" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen30476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30477" type="x-p"/> The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the Jews - Dahler supposes this discourse to have been delivered in the seventeenth or eighteenth year after the taking of Jerusalem. <div eID="gen30477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30478" type="x-p"/> Which dwell at Migdol - A city of Lower Egypt, not far from Pelusium. <div eID="gen30478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30479" type="x-p"/> Tahpanhes - Daphne Pelusiaca, the place to which the emigrant Jews first went. <div eID="gen30479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30480" type="x-p"/> Noph - מפס Maphes, Targum. Memphis. a celebrated city of Middle Egypt, and the capital of its district. <div eID="gen30480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30481" type="x-p"/> The country of Pathros - A district of Upper Egypt, known by the name of the Thebais. See Bochart, Lib. Phaleg, lib. iv., c. 22. Thus we find that the Jews were scattered over the principal parts of Egypt.
entries.d0f04526dca8f23924a9d9590eae2faaf62a80e3: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen30481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30482" type="x-p"/> No man dwelleth therein - The desolation of the land of Judea must have been exceedingly great when this, in almost any sense, could be spoken of it.
entries.fd70828e17b242a44b9a0da4a2f72461da0f0840: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen30482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30483" type="x-p"/> O, do not this abominable thing - A strong specimen of affectionate entreaty. One of the finest figures of poetry, when judiciously managed, the anthropopathia, the ascribing human passions to God, is often used by this prophet: so God is said to grieve, to mourn, to have his bowels moved with compassion, to repent, to be angry, etc. Here he is represented as tenderly expostulating: O, do not; or, I entreat you, do not that abominable thing which I hate. <div eID="gen30483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30484" type="x-p"/> 1. Do it not: your God commands. <div eID="gen30484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30485" type="x-p"/> 2. O, do it not: your Father entreats. <div eID="gen30485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30486" type="x-p"/> 3. It is an abominable thing, and should not be done. <div eID="gen30486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30487" type="x-p"/> 4. I hate it, and on that account ye should abstain from it.
entries.23b32cba402a507b101b6951cec20a2a8bf5d7f6: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen30487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30488" type="x-p"/> But they hearkened not - <div eID="gen30488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30489" type="x-p"/> 1. They disregarded the authority of their God. <div eID="gen30489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30490" type="x-p"/> 2. They were not moved by the entreaties of their most affectionate Father. <div eID="gen30490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30491" type="x-p"/> 3. In abominations they delighted. And, <div eID="gen30491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30492" type="x-p"/> 4. They loved that which God hated; and, apparently, because he hated it.
entries.68896397b04b9b61c7db54a1c28bec83bff9291e: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen30492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30493" type="x-p"/> This great evil against your souls - Will not self-interest weigh with you? See what ruin your conduct has brought upon your country. Your fathers sinned as you are doing; and where are they now? Either destroyed, or in captivity. And you are now taking the same way to your own destruction.
entries.f19e9aac17cbc82d6c6402af9d24ecae7f2cd3c0: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen30493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30494" type="x-p"/> Have ye forgotten the wickedness of your fathers - It seems that the women were principal agents in idolatrous practices; for the queens - the wives, of rulers and of common people, burnt incense to the queen of heaven, (the moon), <reference osisRef="Jer.44.17">Jer 44:17</reference>, and poured out drink-offerings to her.
entries.8cadd3b5c3ba91640e3558e61e6f5515e3302064: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen30494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30495" type="x-p"/> Then all the men - and all the women - We have not seen the women in determined rebellion before. Here they make a common cause with their idolatrous husbands.
entries.08667ac6fa9cc4d6862d694312723826b96d4926: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen30495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30496" type="x-p"/> And when we burned incense to the queen of heaven - The Moon seems to have been called מלכת melecheth, as the sun was called מלך molech. The Hindoos pour out water to the sun thrice a day; and to the moon whenever they worship her. <div eID="gen30496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30497" type="x-p"/> The idolatrous worship of these people was a sort of imitation of the worship of the true God; only sacrifice was not common in it. The factious women here tell us in what it consisted. <div eID="gen30497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30498" type="x-p"/> 1. They burnt incense to the moon, and perhaps to the sun and the planets. <div eID="gen30498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30499" type="x-p"/> 2. They poured out libations to her. <div eID="gen30499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30500" type="x-p"/> 3. They made and consecrated cakes to her. <div eID="gen30500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30501" type="x-p"/> All these were prescribed in the worship of the true God. See, among others, <reference osisRef="Exo.29.23">Exo 29:23</reference>, etc.; <reference osisRef="Lev.2.4">Lev 2:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.23.16">Lev 23:16</reference>; and <reference osisRef="Num.6.15">Num 6:15</reference>. And the women vindicate their conduct by asserting that they did all this by the consent of their husbands: "Did we worship her without our men?"
entries.8f4132500d739b87242ed3ee2a0dcb0bb5d2acc5: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen30501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30502" type="x-p"/> Therefore is your land a desolation - I grant that ye and your husbands have joined together in these abominations; and what is the consequence? "The Lord could no longer bear because of your evil doings; and therefore is your land a desolation, and an astonishment, and a curse, without an inhabitant, this day."
entries.5dc16d03d33127aab2e0c41df092ee9532035e9f: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen30502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30503" type="x-p"/> Behold I will give Pharaoh-hophra - That is, Pharaoh Apries. How this and the prophecies in the preceding chapter were fulfilled, we learn from ancient historians. The sum of such information is this: the subjects of Pharaoh Apries rebelling, he sent Amasis, one of his generals, to reduce them to their duty. But no sooner had Amasis begun to make his speech, than they fixed a helmet on his head, and proclaimed him king. Amasis accepted the title, and confirmed the Egyptians in their revolt; and the greater part of the nation declaring for him, Apries was obliged to retire into Upper Egypt; and the country being thus weakened by intestine war, was attacked and easily overcome by Nebuchadnezzar, who on quitting it left Amasis his viceroy. After Nebuchadnezzar's departure, Apries marched against Amasis; but, being defeated at Memphis, was taken prisoner, carried to Sais, and was strangled in his own palace, thus verifying this prophecy. See Herodotus in Euterpe. <div eID="gen30503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30504" type="x-p"/> Thus Nebuchadnezzar made an easy conquest of the land. He conquered it as easily as "a shepherd puts on his cloak: he went thence in peace," having clothed himself with its spoils; and left all quiet under a viceroy of his own choosing. The rebellion of Pharaoh's subjects was the "fire that God kindled in Egypt," <reference osisRef="Jer.43.12">Jer 43:12</reference>. And thus was he "delivered into the hands of his enemies," his revolted people; and "into the hand of him who sought his life," i.e., Amasis his general. And thus the whole prophecy was literally fulfilled.  <chapter eID="Jer.44"/> <div eID="gen30504" type="x-p"/>

entries.445f4282af99c29ba2767649a100bba099da320f: <reference osisRef="Jer.44.1">Jer 44:1</reference> <hi type="italic">"The word that came to Jeremiah regarding all the Jews who were living in the land of Egypt, who dwelt in Migdol, in Tahpanhes, in Noph, and in the land of Pathros."</hi> From this heading we perceive that those who (according to <reference osisRef="Jer.43.1-Jer.43.13">Jer 43:1-13</reference>) had gone to Egypt, had settled there in various parts of the country, and that the following denunciations, which at the same time form his last prophecy, were uttered a long time after that which is given in <reference osisRef="Jer.43.8-Jer.43.13">Jer 43:8-13</reference> as having been delivered at Tahpanhes. The date of it cannot, indeed, be determined exactly. From the threatening that King Hophra shall be delivered over to the power of Nebuchadnezzar (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.24-Jer.44.30">Jer 44:24-30</reference>), only this much is clear, that Egypt was not yet occupied by the Chaldeans, which, as we have shown above (p. 353), did not take place before the year 572. But it by no means follows from this that Jeremiah did not utter these words of threatening till shortly before this event. He may have done so even five or ten years before, in the period between 585 and 580, as we have already observed on p. 12. The Jews had settled down, not merely in the two northern frontier towns, <hi type="italic">Migdol</hi> (i.e., <hi type="italic">Magdolo</hi>, Μαγδώλος, according to the <hi type="italic">Itiner. Anton.</hi>, twelve Roman miles from Pelusium, Copt. <hi type="italic">Meschtôl</hi>, Egypt. <hi type="italic">Ma'ktr</hi>, the most northerly place in Egypt; see on <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.10">Eze 29:10</reference>) and <hi type="italic">Tahpanhes</hi> (i.e., <hi type="italic">Daphne</hi>, see on <reference osisRef="Jer.43.7">Jer 43:7</reference>), but also in more inland places, in <hi type="italic">Noph</hi> (i.e., <hi type="italic">Memphis</hi>, see on <reference osisRef="Jer.2.16">Jer 2:16</reference>) and the land of <hi type="italic">Pathros</hi> (lxx Παθούρης, Egypt. <hi type="italic">Petorees</hi>, i.e., <hi type="italic">Southland</hi>, viz., Upper Egypt, the <hi type="italic">Thebais</hi> of the Greeks and Romans; see on <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.14">Eze 29:14</reference>). The word of the Lord runs as follows: -
entries.d9f6fae87b56ddfda463f5111fa0a9c1e558d777: <reference osisRef="Jer.44.2-Jer.44.14">Jer 44:2-14</reference> <hi type="italic">The warning and threatening. - "Thus saith Jahveh of hosts, the God of Israel: Ye yourselves have been all the evil which I have brought on Jerusalem, and on all the cities of Judah; and, behold, they are a desolation this day, and there is no inhabitant in them;</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.44.3">Jer 44:3</reference> <hi type="italic">. Because of their wickedness which they have done, by provoking me through going to burn incense, (and) to serve other gods whom they knew not, (neither) they (nor) ye, nor your fathers.</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.44.4">Jer 44:4</reference> <hi type="italic">. And I sent unto you all my servants the prophets, rising early and sending (them), to say, Do not this abominable thing which I hate.</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.44.5">Jer 44:5</reference> <hi type="italic">. But they did not hear, nor inclined their ear to turn from their wickedness, by not burning incense to other gods.</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.44.6">Jer 44:6</reference> <hi type="italic">. Therefore my wrath and mine anger poured itself out, and burned up the cities of Judah and the streets of Jerusalem; so that they have become a desolation and a waste, as at this day.</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.44.7">Jer 44:7</reference> <hi type="italic">. Now therefore thus saith Jahveh of hosts, the God of Israel: Why do ye great evil against your souls, by cutting off from yourselves man and women, child and suckling, out of the midst of Judah, so leaving no remnant for yourselves;</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.44.8">Jer 44:8</reference> <hi type="italic">. Through provoking me by the works of your hands, burning incense to other gods in the land of Egypt, whither ye have gone to sojourn, that ye might bring destruction on yourselves, and that ye might become a curse and a reproach among all the nations of the earth?</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.44.9">Jer 44:9</reference> <hi type="italic">. Have ye forgotten the evil deeds of your fathers, and the evil deeds of the kings of Judah, and the evil deeds of their wives, and your own evil deeds, and the evil deeds of your wives, which they committed in the land of Judah and on the streets of Jerusalem?</hi> Jer 44:10. <hi type="italic">They have not been contrite to this day, and are not afraid, nor do they walk in my law, and in my statutes, which I have set before you and before your fathers.</hi> Jer 44:11. <hi type="italic">Therefore thus saith Jahveh of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will set my face against you for evil, and to cut off all Judah.</hi> Jer 44:12. <hi type="italic">And I will take the remnant of Judah, that have set their faces to go to the land of Egypt in order to sojourn there, and they shall all be consumed; in the land of Egypt shall they fall, by sword and famine shall they be consumed; small and great, by sword and famine shall they die, and they shall become an execration and an astonishment, and a curse and a reproach.</hi> Jer 44:13. <hi type="italic">And I will punish those who dwell in the land of Egypt, as I punished Jerusalem, by sword, and famine, and pestilence.</hi> Jer 44:14. <hi type="italic">There shall not be one escaped or left to the remnant of Judah that came to sojourn there in the land of Egypt, so as to return to the land of Judah, whither they long to return and dwell; for they shall not return except as escaped ones."</hi>  <reference osisRef="Jer.44.2-Jer.44.6">Jer 44:2-6</reference> <div eID="gen14336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14337" type="x-p"/> In order to make an impression on the people by his warning against idolatry, Jeremiah begins his address with a reference to the great calamity which the fathers have brought on the kingdom of Judah through their continued idolatry (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.2-Jer.44.6">Jer 44:2-6</reference>). "Ye have seen all the evil," etc.; all the cities are laid waste and depopulated, because their inhabitants have roused the anger of the Lord, and have not let themselves be dissuaded by the admonitions of the prophets whom God has sent. "This day," i.e., now, at present. On <reference osisRef="Jer.44.3">Jer 44:3</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.11.17">Jer 11:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.19.4">Jer 19:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.32.32">Jer 32:32</reference>, etc.; and as to the meaning of קטּר, see on Jer 1:16. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Jer.44.3">Jer 44:3</reference></hi> the address becomes more direct, through the change into the second person, "ye;" the audience then present only continue these sins of their fathers. On <reference osisRef="Jer.44.4">Jer 44:4</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.7.25">Jer 7:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.25.4">Jer 25:4</reference>, etc. דּבר התּעבה הזּאת, "the thing of this abomination," which is equivalent to "this abominable idolatry." דּבר serves to render the subject more prominent, as in Jdg 19:24. On <reference osisRef="Jer.44.6">Jer 44:6</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.42.18">Jer 42:18</reference>; Jer 7:20. The wrath of God burned in the cities, for the fire of destruction was a manifestation of the divine wrath. As to כּיום הזּה, see on Jer 11:5.
entries.592ce42490a305b4a3977419e16cd57f3d7f58c9: <reference osisRef="Jer.44.15-Jer.44.19">Jer 44:15-19</reference> <hi type="italic">The answer of the people to this threatening address.</hi> - Jer 44:15. <hi type="italic">"Then all the men who knew that their wives burned incense to other gods, and all the women standing [there], a great multitude, and all the people who dwelt in the land of Egypt, in Pathros, answered Jeremiah, saying, </hi> Jer 44:16. <hi type="italic">[As for] the word which thou hast spoken unto us in the name of Jahveh, we will not hearken unto thee: </hi> Jer 44:17. <hi type="italic">But we will certainly perform every word that has proceeded out of our own mouth, by burning incense to the queen of heaven, and pouring out libations to her, just as we have done, we and our fathers, our kings and our princes, in the cities of Judah, and in the streets of Jerusalem; and we were filled with bread, and became prosperous, and saw no evil. </hi> Jer 44:18. <hi type="italic">But since we ceased to offer incense to the queen of heaven, and to pour out libations to her, we have been in want of everything, and are consumed by sword and famine. </hi> Jer 44:19. <hi type="italic">And when we [women] have been burning incense to the queen of heaven, and poured out libations to her, have we made cakes to her without our husbands, making an image of her, and offering libations to her?"</hi> To the word of the prophet the men and women oppose their pretended experience, that the adoration of the queen of heaven has brought them comfort and prosperity, while the neglect of this worship, on the other hand, has brought want and misfortune. No doubt they inferred this, by the argument <hi type="italic">post hoc, ergo propter hoc</hi>, from the fact that, after idolatry had been rooted out by Josiah, adversity had befallen the land of Judah; while, up till that time, the kingdom of Judah had been independent, and, for more than a century before, had been spared the suffering of misfortune. Thus, through their blindness, peculiar to the natural man, they had overlooked the minor transient evils with which the Lord visits His people when they sin. Not till near the end of Josiah’s reign did misfortune fall on Judah: this was when the Egyptian army, under Pharaoh-Necho, marched through Palestine; Josiah was slain in the battle he had lost, the land was laid waste by the enemy, and its inhabitants perished by sword and famine. In <reference osisRef="Jer.44.15">Jer 44:15</reference>, those who are represented speaking are all the men who knew of their wives’ idolatry, i.e., who permitted it, and all the women, "a great company," i.e., gathered together in great numbers, and all the rest of the people who lived in Egypt. The specification "in Pathros" is not in apposition to the words "in the land of Egypt," but belongs to the verb ויּענוּ; it tells where the gathering took place, viz., in a district of Upper Egypt. From the presence of a large number of women, we may conclude that the assembly was a festival in honour of the queen of heaven. The former portion of <reference osisRef="Jer.44.16">Jer 44:16</reference> forms an absolute clause, from הדּבר to בּשׁם, "as regards the word which...we will not listen to thee," i.e., with regard to this word we obey thee not. The expression, "the word which has gone forth out of our mouth," points to the uttering of vows: cf. Num 30:13; Deu 23:24. 'כּל־הדּבר means "all that we have uttered as a vow," every vow to offer incense, etc., i.e., to present meat and drink offerings to the queen of heaven, - that shall we keep, fulfil, as we and our fathers have done in the land of Judah. On this mode of worship, cf. Jer 7:17., and the remarks there made. "And we were satisfied with bread," i.e., in consequence of this worship we had amply sufficient food. Towbiym טובים, "good," well, comfortable; cf. Jer 22:16. מן אז, "from that time" = since. תּמנוּ is for תּמּנוּ, from תּמם, as in Num 17:1-13 :28; cf. Ewald, §197, <hi type="italic">a</hi>. To this statement on the part of the men, the women further add, <reference osisRef="Jer.44.19">Jer 44:19</reference>, that they do not engage in this sacrificial worship or prepare the sacrificial cakes without their husbands, i.e., without their knowledge and approval. This is put forward by the women in the way of self-vindication; for, according to the law, Num 30:9., the husband could annul, i.e., declare not binding, any vow which had been made by his wife without his knowledge. Although it is women who are speaking, the <hi type="italic">masc</hi>. מקטּרים is used as being the gender which most commonly occurs; it also pretty often stands for the feminine. The <hi type="italic">inf. constr.</hi> וּלהסּך (with ל) is here employed, in conformity with later usage, instead of the <hi type="italic">inf. abs.</hi>, for the finite verb, by way of continuation; cf. Ewald, §351, <hi type="italic">c</hi>, where, however, many passages have been set down as falling under this rule that demand a different explanation. The meaning of להעצבה is disputed; the final ה is a suffix, written with Raphe, though Mappik also occurs in some MSS. The Hiphil of this verb is found elsewhere only in <reference osisRef="Ps.78.40">Psa 78:40</reference>, and there in the signification of vexing, grieving, like the Piel in <reference osisRef="Isa.63.10">Isa 63:10</reference>; Psa 66:6. Ewald translates "in order to move her," i.e., make her well-disposed, - but quite arbitrarily, for to provoke is the very opposite of rendering propitious. The verb עצּב also signifies "to form, shape," <reference osisRef="Job.10.8">Job 10:8</reference>; and in this sense the Hiphil is used here, "in order to put them into shape," i.e., to form the moon-goddess (queen of heaven) in or on the sacrificial cakes (Kimchi, Raschi, Dahler, Maurer, Graf, etc.). The sacrificial cakes (כּוּנים, see on <reference osisRef="Jer.7.18">Jer 7:18</reference>) probably had the form of a crescent, or even of the full moon, like the σελῆναι of the Greeks, which used to be offered in Athens at the time of the full moon in the month of Munychion, to Artemis, as goddess of the moon; cf. Hermann, <hi type="italic">gottesdienstliche Alterthümer der Griechen</hi>, 2 Ausg. S. 146, Anm. 13, u. S. 414.
